processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: SPCC sheet (thickness 1.2 mm) pre-strained to 15% by tensile deformation; this is specimen condition/species 'B' in Table 1. Plastic deformation releases dislocations from the Cottrell atmosphere so that they become movable.

structures.overall_structure: 15% pre-strained mild steel (SPCC) in which dislocations originally locked by carbon/solutes via the Cottrell effect have been released by plastic deformation; the dislocation structure changes with plastic strain and the released (movable) dislocations pile up near grain boundaries.

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Dislocations released from a common source move along the same slip surface and pile up against obstacles such as grain boundaries and solutes; the pile-up causes deformation during unloading and during loading at stresses below the yield stress, so that the apparent elastic modulus decreases as a function of plastic strain (Fig. 3 pile-up model).

interfaces.slip_behavior: Dislocations move along the same slip surface and easily pile up, the front of the dislocations being stopped by obstacles such as grain boundaries and solutes; the pile-up dislocations can move backwards when the shear stress is released during unloading.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Tensile test using a load cell and strain gauge; elastic modulus of species B calculated from the initial stage (strain 0–0.05%); no unit is printed for the modulus in Table 2.
Tensile test using a load cell and strain gauge; elastic modulus of species B calculated over the whole elastic range; no unit is printed for the modulus in Table 2.
Apparent modulus (gradient of the stress–strain curve) over the elastic/near-elastic region up to 0.3% strain, read from Fig. 4(b); values read from gridlines, no numeric data labels printed.

youngs_modulus.value: from ~200 GPa (near 0.05% strain) decreasing to below 50 GPa (at 0.3% strain)

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Fig. 4(a): stress–strain curves up to 0.3% strain for species A–E; species B is one of the fan-out curves.

characterization_methods.technique: precision tensile test (stress–strain measurement) with strain gauge / precision extensometer
characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: load cell and strain gauge; precision extensometer developed by the authors
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: stress–strain curve measured up to 1% strain, then elastic modulus obtained from the stress–strain curves within the elastic deformation region; used for the pre-strained specimens of Table 1 (species A–E)
characterization_methods.purpose: measure the stress–strain curve and the elastic modulus of the pre-strained and heat-treated specimens before/after plastic deformation to confirm the effect of movable dislocations
characterization_methods.key_findings: the gradient of the stress–strain curve decreases from the beginning up to the macroscopic yield point, so the modulus varies significantly for the 15% pre-strain specimen B; the modulus measured over 0–0.05% strain always exceeds that over the whole elastic range

unmapped_findings: Table 2 of the paper does not print units for the elastic modulus; the values 188 (0–0.05% strain) and 162 (whole elastic range) for species B are unitless in the source table.

General finding reported for the (SPCE) sheet metal of section 2: Young's modulus decreases with plastic strain, the decrease being more than 20% after a deformation of 25% plastic strain; the elastic modulus variation is fitted as E = E0*(351ε² − 160ε + 93.8) (Fig. 1). This is based on SPCE, not on the SPCC specimen B.
The heat-treatment condition of 373 K for 90 h (to recover only the Cottrell atmosphere by C diffusion while keeping dislocations stationary) was applied to specimens C and D, not to species B.

The nano-indentation experiments (Figs. 7–12) were performed on the SPCE specimen (specimen outline labelled 'SPCE' in Fig. 10), not on the SPCC specimen B, so those near-grain-boundary modulus results are not attributed to this sample.
